rows: If you are a domestic dog, you have two kinds of cone, one most sensitive near 555 nm and one near 430 nm. Yellows and blues reach you clearly while reds and greens come close together.
If you are a domestic dog, your rod cells peak near 508 nm and take over when the light fades. If you are a coyote, your retina holds many more rods than cones.
Dogs have a reflecting layer behind the retina, and in a domestic dog it throws light back. You very likely gather more of a dim scene because of it.
Dogs take in about 240 degrees around them, with an overlap of 30 to 60 degrees straight ahead. You very likely see most of the world beside you at once.

Dogs see up to four times less fine detail than humans. If you are a domestic dog or a wolf, your sharpest sight lies along a horizontal streak, pronounced or moderate, with an oval patch of dense cells in it.
A painted dog's pupil is round, and a domestic dog's pupil is described as round too. You very likely have a round pupil.
A flickering light merged into steady light at about 75 flashes a second in tests on domestic dogs. You very likely follow quick change in fine slices of time.

Nobody has given your sharpness as a number of cycles per degree, how strongly colors register for you, how fast sharpness falls from the center of your streak, how much brighter dim scenes look through your mirror layer, how bright your eye shine is, or how much ultraviolet reaches you, though both cone kinds respond to it. The light levels where your rods take over are also unmeasured.
Nobody has measured some parts of how you see, so they are guesses.

On this trial the colours come from the dog's two measured cone pigments. The camera's colours and the display are the app's.
As the light falls, the colours drift toward what the dog's rods take in, which peak near 508 nm. The peak is measured; where the change happens is the app's guess.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: Your eyesight is much blurrier than a human's. If you are a domestic dog, you see about a third or less of the fine detail a human sees.
rows.note: The approved row of VOICE.md said 'a quarter or less'; Lind 2017 tested dogs and humans in one apparatus and found humans about three times sharper (cat-dog#172), and reviews give four to seven times (cat-dog#118), so 'a third or less' covers the measurements. Red fox 6.3 and arctic fox 9.2 cycles a degree support the first sentence.
rows.rewrite_reason: Use VOICE.md's approved dog Sharpness row. The draft's 20/75 explanation and 'a review cites an estimate' run long on a phone.

rows.title: Sharpest spot
rows.text: If you have a long nose, like a wolf, a red fox or a whippet, you see most sharply along a band level with the horizon. If you have a short nose, like a pug, you see most sharply in one spot in the middle.
rows.note: The approved row of VOICE.md with 'greyhound' replaced by species and a breed the records name (the wolf in McGreevy 2003, the red fox in Malkemper 2018, the whippet in Lind 2017). The arctic fox also has a band (intake-4#18). No record covers the gray fox. Graded m as approved; rows.py computes i (42% measured, 58% unknown), since the coyote and gray fox are unmeasured.
rows.rewrite_reason: Use VOICE.md's approved row. The draft gives the Arctic fox only a spot; its record and the fox view give it a strong band.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: You have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where humans have three. A blue-green that looks like a clear color to a human looks gray to you.
rows.note: The approved row of VOICE.md. The record the drafter lacked is logged already: cat-dog#68 (Miller 2001, trait colour_vision) gives the dog's neutral point near 480 nm, seen as white or gray.
rows.rewrite_reason: Use VOICE.md's approved Color row; the draft's second sentence repeats the first. Log a record for 'blue-green looks gray'; the drafter found none.

rows.title: Field of view, dim light and depth
rows.text: If you are a domestic dog, a review estimates that you take in about 240 degrees around you, where a human takes in 180, and that your two eyes overlap by 30 to 60 degrees. In dim light you have more rods than a human, even in the center of the retina where a human has none, and about 7 in 10 dogs examined had a full-sized tapetum, the mirror layer behind the retina, while a few had none. Nobody has measured how well you judge depth.
rows.note: Dropped the 539 count and the 2 percent figure. The depth sentence rests on no record, because R5 is a cat record on focusing range.
